## End-to-end launch process

1. **Create the intake ticket.** The requester—typically Product or Solutions Engineering—opens a Linear ticket in **ENG** labeled `model-onboarding`. The ticket records model name/version and type, upstream source, tokenizer and special tokens, proposed Redwood ID and compatibility target, license and redistribution status, restrictions, safety/data concerns, target workloads, regions, and SLOs. The ticket is the single source of truth for the intake summary. [2][4]

2. **Complete the three intake gates before proceeding.**
   - **License pre-check — Finance-Legal liaison + Security:** decide `approved`, `approved w/ restrictions`, or `blocked`; record a link to the Security risk-review entry. [2][3]
   - **Baseline evaluation plan — Applied ML:** select suites and success criteria; record the plan in a Linear comment and link the eval-harness runs. Readiness requires at least one internal prompt set and one public benchmark. [2][3]
   - **Feasibility/runtime fit — Serving Runtime:** confirm tokenizer handling, KV-cache behavior, and kernel coverage; provide a feasibility note and any required runtime flags. [2][3]

3. **Run the Security & Compliance risk review.** **Security & Compliance (Risk & Exceptions)** reviews upstream provenance, license terms, maintainers/vendor relationship, and customer constraints. Required checks are artifact checksum and exact tag/commit recording (hashes go in the registry change description); supply-chain scanning of images/build environment, malware scanning of archives, and approval or review of conversion scripts; confirmation of hosted-serving redistribution rights and communication of restrictions; privacy and data-handling checks; and policy-layer compatibility. High-risk models require Product signoff and staged rollout. The artifact is a risk-review entry listing risks, mitigations, restrictions, and a decision of `approved`, `approved-with-restrictions`, or `blocked`; restricted approvals must include exact restriction text for docs. [5]
   
   Exceptions such as unclear provenance or incomplete upstream documentation require a Security exception record and VP Engineering approval, linked from both the Linear intake ticket and GitHub model-registry PR. [5]

4. **Confirm readiness for implementation.** Proceed only when the license is approved (or approved with documented restrictions), the evaluation plan includes an internal prompt set and a public benchmark, the runtime owner reports no known blockers, and a rollout owner is named for release and platform. [2][3]

5. **Evaluate and assemble launch artifacts.**
   - **Public benchmark sanity:** use curated public tasks such as MMLU, GSM8K, or HumanEval subsets. No task may drop more than 5% absolute versus upstream numbers after adjusting for Redwood settings; if upstream numbers are unavailable, compare adjacent family sizes and explain outliers. Artifact: score table and notes. [1]
   - **Safety and policy screening:** check policy prompts and refusal behavior; there must be no increase in disallowed content, and refusal templates must work with the Redwood policy layer. Artifact: pass/fail summary and policy configuration notes. [1]
   - **Tool/function calling, if marketed for it:** require at least 99% JSON-schema conformance on the tool-calling prompt set. Artifact: schema-validation report link. [1]
   - **Launch packet:** include eval-harness run URLs for all required suites, a one-paragraph production risk assessment, recommended default temperature/top-p/max-tokens settings, and known limitations. [1]
   - **Other intake artifacts:** performance benchmark results and run IDs go in the Performance Standards page; quantization plan/results go in the Quantization Profiles space; security review goes in Security & Compliance; rollout/fallback plan goes in the Eng Platform runbook; and the model-registry change is a GitHub PR in `redwood-model-registry`. [2]

6. **Apply launch gates and exceptions.** Exceptions to evaluation gates need approval from the Applied ML gate owner and an `eval-exception` label on the Linear ticket. Do not ship if Suite A fails on any `p0` prompt. [1]

7. **Monitor after launch.** For the first **7 days after GA**, enable a 1% quality canary shadowed against baseline where possible, watch the `quality_regression_alerts` dashboard and error-budget burn, and file a follow-up ticket if a metric crosses the Platform runbook thresholds. [1]

The intake source names the requester, Applied ML, Serving Runtime, Release Engineering, Security & Compliance, and DevEx/Docs roles; it specifies Release and Platform owners for readiness, but does not assign a separate owner for every individual evaluation or post-launch monitoring task. [2][3][4]

## Required production rollout plan

For a new model version receiving production traffic, use the canonical rollout template. The plan should be the source of truth during an incident; mark inapplicable sections “N/A” with a brief justification. [2][3][1]

1. **Summary:** What is changing, why now, expected customer impact (best- and worst-case), and the rollout point person and Slack channel. [3]

2. **Scope:** Hosted, Dedicated, and/or Private environments; affected regions; customer tiers or allowlists; and applicable request types (chat, completions, embeddings, rerank). [1][3]

3. **Versioning and compatibility:** Model alias, new version identifier, backward-compatibility notes (including tool calling, output formatting, and tokenization), and maximum context/output token limits. [1][3]

4. **Success criteria and guardrails:** Define explicit pass/fail thresholds, owners, and evaluation windows. Cover reliability (5xx rate, timeouts, admission rejects), latency (p50/p95 end-to-end and streaming time-to-first-token), cost/efficiency (tokens/sec/GPU, cache-hit rate, batch efficiency), and quality (eval regression and customer-reported issues). [1][3] The template’s examples—not universal mandated limits—include p95 latency over 30 minutes passing at no more than +5% versus baseline and failing above +10%; 5xx rate over 30 minutes passing at no more than +0.05 percentage points absolute and failing above +0.2 points; and quality per run passing at baseline −0.3 or better and failing below baseline −0.7. [1][3]

5. **Monitoring:** Link service/model/region dashboards; list alerts and trace/log queries; assign owners for monitoring at each ramp step. Confirm dashboards and alerts are configured and owned for the rollout. [1][2]

6. **Rollout steps:** Document canary percentage and duration, signals and decision points for advancing, ramp schedule and timestamps, and blast-radius controls such as customer allowlists, per-region traffic caps, and concurrency caps. Include experiment details if using an A/B test. [1][3]

7. **Rollback and fallback:** Specify rollback triggers mapped to the plan’s thresholds, the rollback procedure/runbook, automatic versus manual actions, fallback target versions, ordering and constraints, and treatment of in-flight requests and streaming responses. Test the rollback path in staging or a performance canary before the change. [1][2]

8. **Customer communications:** Identify customers, channels, timing, message content, and approval/tracking details, as specified below. [1][4]

9. **Approvals and change window:** Record change class, approvers and timestamps, and approved window. [1][2] Hosted and Dedicated changes are preferably Tuesday–Thursday, 09:00–14:00 PT unless explicitly approved; Private changes must align with and document each customer’s window. [2]

10. **Post-rollout validation:** Record final KPIs after full ramp, customer feedback, follow-up tasks, and owners. Within 48 hours of completing the rollout, add an outcome note with final ramp percentage, issues, and follow-ups, and file tasks for threshold violations or customer escalations. [1][2]

## Approvals and change controls

Class 1 covers canaries of up to 5% traffic with immediate rollback; Class 2 includes impact above 5%, a new default version, or safety/tool-calling/formatting changes; Class 3 covers global default changes, broad impact, or changes that could violate contracts or compliance commitments. [2] Required approvers are: **Class 1**—Oncall Engineering Manager for the affected service or Platform Engineering TL; **Class 2**—Platform Engineering Manager, SRE on-call delegate, and Inference Product Manager; **Class 3**—VP Engineering or delegate, Security if policy/compliance is implicated, and Product Director or higher. [2] For Private deployments, add Solutions Engineering lead and Private Deployments Engineering TL; for SLA/contract impact, Customer Success Director; for data-residency/retention impact, Security & Compliance. [2]

Before the change, publish and link the plan from the change ticket, ensure dashboards and alerts are configured and owned, test rollback, and confirm blast-radius controls are available. [2]

## Customer-facing communications

Always notify Dedicated customers receiving the new version as default and impacted Private customers. Notify Hosted customers when a commonly used alias has a material change to output format/tool calling, context or output limits, latency/reliability expectations, or safety behavior. [4] Timing: Dedicated customers at least 5 business days before the window unless they agree otherwise; Private customers according to contract, defaulting to 10 business days before maintenance; Hosted customers at least 72 hours beforehand for material behavior changes, otherwise release notes are sufficient. [4] Use email to customer technical contacts plus a tracking support ticket for Dedicated/Private; use release notes for Hosted, with optional email to top impacted organizations. Use status-page rules for incidents or wide impact. ## End-to-end emergency serving-runtime hotfix

### 1. Confirm the emergency and prepare
- Use the emergency process for an active Sev-1/Sev-2 incident, credible imminent outage, or security issue; declare an incident for active customer impact and coordinate in its incident channel. [2][3]
- Confirm customer impact and blast radius, rollout targets (regions, tiers, routes, or Dedicated clusters), monitoring availability, and a redeployable rollback version and procedure. [2][3]
- Open the required dashboards before changing anything: request success rate, latency, runtime restarts/crash loops, GPU utilization and queue depth, and runtime error codes. [2]
- Create or link a ticket, and record the fix hypothesis, blast radius, rollback trigger, risks, change type, and post-change monitoring owner. [5]

### 2. Obtain approvals
- For a Hosted serving-runtime change, obtain approval from the IC or Primary SRE Oncall **and** Serving Runtime Engineering Oncall or Runtime EM. Record approvals in the incident channel, PR, or change record. [3][5]
- For a Dedicated rollout, also obtain Dedicated Service Owner approval and Customer Success escalation manager sign-off on customer messaging. [4]
- Add Security Oncall approval for a security-related or suspected exploit change; add Product Oncall or the responsible PM for customer-visible behavior changes. [5]
- Keep a rollback plan and emergency approvals documented; do not bundle unrelated changes into the same emergency change. [1][5]

### 3. Implement, review, and build
- Create `hotfix/runtime-<YYYYMMDD>-<short-issue>`, cherry-pick only the minimum fix, and update the Runtime Hotfixes changelog. [1]
- Open a PR targeting the release branch, or `main` if no release branch is available. Get review from Runtime Oncall and SRE Oncall (or the IC); include the incident link, hypothesis, risk, rollback plan, and rollout owners. [1]
- Build and sign the runtime image (multi-architecture if applicable), CycloneDX SBOM, and provenance attestation. [1]

### 4. Validate before rollout
- Run affected-module unit tests, one representative-model perf canary, and a stress test matching the incident-triggering sequence length and concurrency. Record results in the PR. [1]
- Check that the triggering error improves or disappears, p95 latency does not regress by more than 10% versus the previous image on the same workload, and OOM/GPU reset counters do not increase. [1]
- For the production change record, document the rollback trigger explicitly, along with the hypothesis, blast radius, risk assessment, change details, and monitoring owner. [5]

### 5. Roll out and verify

**Hosted**
- Prefer a one-region canary first. For a hotfix, use a targeted rollout; the Hosted runbook’s specified rollback sequence is one canary cell in us-east, full us-east, one canary cell in eu-west, then full eu-west. [2]
- At each rollout step, verify success rate, p95 latency, restarts, and error signatures before proceeding; the rollback runbook requires 5xx to return to baseline, p95 to improve or remain flat with no more than 10% regression, restarts to trend down, and no new dominant error signature. [2]
- Post the image tag, expected rollout impact (including restarts or brief connection resets), canary target, and rollback criteria in the incident channel. [1]

**Dedicated**
- Before scheduling, gather customer name and cluster ID, current and target image tags, expected restart impact, rollback tag, and whether the issue is customer-specific or global. [4]
- Canary one Dedicated cluster first, preferably internal dogfood or the lowest-traffic customer with CSEM approval. Validate for 30 minutes: success rate, p95 latency, GPU OOMs, restart frequency, and customer-specific health checks. [4]
- For each cluster, confirm customer communication is sent (unless the IC waives it during an active outage), update `runtime_image_tag`, apply via the cluster’s ArgoCD runtime app, monitor for rollout completion and no CrashLoopBackOff, then run chat, embeddings, and streaming-completion smoke checks. Do not roll out to more than three clusters in parallel unless the IC approves. [4]

### 6. Customer communications, rollback, and closeout
- **Dedicated communications:** For Sev-1, follow the Sev-1 communication requirements; additionally, tell customers if runtime pods will restart and brief interruptions may occur, give an approximate time window, and explain rollback criteria in plain language. [4]
- If rollback criteria are met, restore the previous runtime image/tag and restart the deployment if needed; for Dedicated, notify the customer immediately through CSEM. [1][4]
- Record what changed, where, and the observed effect in the incident channel and timeline; record Dedicated outcomes cluster by cluster, and promote the hotfix into the regular release. [2][4]
- Within two business days, create the incident-review follow-up, document deviations and corrective actions, and remove temporary flags or throttles with an owner and deadline. [5]

The recommended rotation is a **two-phase process: preflight, then cutover**. [3]

1. **Preflight (no live swap):** Create a new KMS key version and point the signing-key alias at it for testing. Enable CI adapters to use the new version in feature-flagged mode, run test signings, and verify the attestation service accepts them. Then run a shadow cross-account copy with the ephemeral role and confirm it succeeds in all target regions. Monitor for 24 hours—or three release windows—for pull-auth regressions. [3]

2. **Cutover:** Schedule a change window, atomically move the signing-key alias to the new version, allow a five-minute grace period, then revoke short-lived CI credentials associated with the old version and rotate ephemeral-role sessions. Promote a canary signed with the new key and check latency and error metrics for 20 minutes; proceed to fleet-wide promotion only if no safety triggers fire. [3]

**Rollback:** If a trigger fires, restore the alias to the old key version and mark the new version revocation-pending for forensic review. For persistent pull-auth problems, the runbook also calls for reverting affected warm pools to the previous production image tag if problems last more than 10 minutes. [3]

## Process

1. **Collect representative production signatures.** Sample route traffic for 1–2 weeks at a configurable 1–5% rate. Capture fields such as sequence length, input/output tokens, KV-cache hit rate, streaming flag, client tier, and model-variant hint. These describe request shape and distribution, which are the basis for workload-specific SLOs. [3][6]

2. **Cluster workload patterns per route.** Run offline clustering—such as k-means or hierarchical clustering—on normalized features including sequence length, total tokens, KV-cache hit rate, streaming status, and concurrency. Aim for 3–6 clusters per route unless the observed variance warrants more; retain centroids and representative percentiles for each cluster. [2][6]

3. **Profile representative clusters in controlled experiments.** Replay about 10,000 representative requests per cluster against relevant model variants and runtime configurations, varying batch sizes, quantization, and kernel paths. Measure latency percentiles (including tail latency), throughput, GPU utilization, memory pressure, failures, and estimated cost per request. [2][6]

4. **Derive and validate SLOs from evidence.** Use profiling results to propose achievable targets with a confidence margin; one example is setting a p95 target at profiling p90 plus a 15% buffer. Validate targets against sampled production telemetry and controlled experiments, and segment SLOs where workload clusters materially differ rather than applying one target to every route. [2][3]

5. **Attach cost-sensitivity guidance to each SLO.** Document how latency and cost change under relevant tradeoffs—such as larger batching, quantization, or a smaller model—and define fallback thresholds where appropriate. This makes the cost impact explicit when adjusting runtime settings or responding to SLO pressure. [2][3]

6. **Operationalize and revalidate.** Publish per-cluster dashboards, alerts, and an experiment plan; monitor SLI trends and cost against targets, then periodically revalidate the SLOs as workload patterns change. [3]

The edge adapter’s lifecycle states are:

- **INIT** — boots and verifies dependencies.
- **REGISTERING** — attempts to join the control plane.
- **ACTIVE** — serves local traffic.
- **DRAINING** — stops accepting new sessions and finishes existing ones.
- **DEGRADED** — continues limited service or redirects to hosted inference when critical resources are missing.
- **RETIRED** — shut down by an operator. [1]

The normal path is **INIT → REGISTERING → ACTIVE**. From **ACTIVE**, an operator or rollout can trigger **DRAINING → RETIRED**. A resource failure can move the service from any state to **DEGRADED**; after recovery, it can return to **ACTIVE**. [1]

The protocol computes a 0–100 Decision Score (DS) from the recent heatmap snapshot:

**DS = clamp(SS + LP + DF, 0, 100)**, where:
- **SS** = 100 × the probe-priority-weighted average of each slice’s failure rate (`failure_count / max(1, total_calls)`).
- **LP** = 10 × the positive amount by which median latency exceeds its SLO, divided by the SLO, capped at 30.
- **DF** = 50 × the 95th-percentile embedding-drift score normalized against baseline drift. [1]

The recommended actions are **DS ≤ 15: proceed (GO); 15 < DS ≤ 35: slow rollout (CAUTION); 35 < DS ≤ 60: pause (HOLD); DS > 60: revert (ROLLBACK).** [1]

This points to a **path-MTU blackhole**, not a model or TLS bug. The transit vendor’s policy change likely began filtering or rate-limiting ICMP “Fragmentation Needed” messages, so the nodes could not learn that the tunnel path’s usable MTU was smaller than their packet size. With DF set across the encapsulated path, oversized packets were dropped and the encrypted streams stalled as TCP retransmitted; large HTTP/2/TLS transfers made the problem especially visible. [1][2][4]

Lowering the node MTU makes packets fit the smaller path MTU, avoiding the blocked PMTU feedback. In a related incident, setting worker MTU to 1400 restored streaming; another reported a temporary MTU reduction restoring artifact pulls. [2][4]

1. **Confirm region and capacity.** The Frankfurt region is called **europe-west3** in the sources. Check regional GPU quota and per-zone GPU availability; one reported check found 8 A100s and 32 T4s available, while another reported only 4 A100s and 50 T4s. 2. **Check network prerequisites.** Confirm subnet IP capacity, shared-VPC permissions, and any VPC Service Controls constraints; ensure pod/node IP ranges have enough room to avoid IP exhaustion during autoscaling. [1][2]

3. **Plan the pools.** For batch workloads, use a preemptible T4 pool and, if needed, an on-demand A100 pool for jobs that should not be interrupted. Apply separate taints and configure batch jobs with matching tolerations. [2]

4. **Configure the managed cluster.** Prefer a regional GKE control plane for high availability, and enable private-cluster networking and VPC-native IP aliasing. [1]

5. **Configure GPU workers.** Set autoscaling minimums and maximums, GPU role/type labels and workload taints; use a GPU-capable machine type and COS Containerd image. Enable GKE GPU driver installation or deploy the driver installer, and ensure the NVIDIA device plugin and other required system components are available. [1][2]

6. **Prepare for preemption and scaling.** Use graceful eviction handling, such as a node termination handler and drain hook; consider PodDisruptionBudgets for critical batch controllers and ensure higher-priority jobs can fall back to on-demand workers. [2]

7. **Validate GPU availability.** Check for NVIDIA-related pods with `kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep nvidia`, then run `nvidia-smi` from a debug pod to confirm the GPU is usable. [1]

### Cause
The 429s were mainly caused by **overload/admission control**, not a billing-quota issue: during regional pressure in us-east, scheduler lag and queue depth rose, and Proxima’s combined chat and embeddings bursts exceeded the conservative enterprise route-group budget. The controls were intended to protect pool stability and latency; enterprise latency remained within SLO during the event. A smaller number of 429s were `quota_exceeded`, including embeddings daily-quota events. [1][7]

### Temporary exception
We applied a **time-boxed burst-multiplier increase** for Proxima’s chat and embeddings routes in us-east, with a **14-day expiry**. It had automated rollback if enterprise p99 latency burn exceeded its threshold or the tenant’s shed rate stayed above 2%; the customer was also required to implement exponential backoff with jitter. [4][6]

### How to verify SLO safety
Monitor the enterprise p95/p99 and SLO-burn dashboards alongside tenant shed rates and 429 reason codes. Confirm the exception is not causing sustained enterprise latency degradation or excessive shedding; the applied guardrails call for rollback at the stated thresholds. The post-change review reported no negative impact on enterprise SLO dashboards. [3][4][6]

## Policy to follow

The sources do not establish a blanket ban on all plaintext DEK caching. The specific ADR-007 policy permits a **restricted, process-local cache** for plaintext DEKs already in memory for request processing: default TTL is 5 minutes, entries must be bounded with LRU eviction, and the cache must be disable-able. Plaintext DEKs must never be persisted or shared across hosts; long-lived caching beyond 15 minutes requires a security exception. [1]

This should be read alongside the Key Management Standard’s instruction to discard plaintext DEKs as soon as possible: retain them only as needed, and apply ADR-007’s limits if using the permitted cache. [1][6] The sources do not show a newer policy that supersedes ADR-007.

- **Fallback is attempted** when overload is detected after the request reaches Smart Routing—such as a routing/runtime overload or breaker-open signal—and the tenant policy permits an eligible fallback. The routing fix also prevents a bookkeeping bug from suppressing valid fallback attempts. Smart Routing makes at most one fallback attempt by default and returns the original overload response if fallback is disallowed or also overloaded. [1][4][5]
- **A gateway-level admission shed** (for example, breaker-open or a concurrency-cap shed) happens before Smart Routing is invoked. In the described behavior, the gateway returns a terminal `503 OVERLOADED`; the configured fallback is not attempted. [2][5][6]
- **Support guidance:** Explain that fallback is best-effort, not guaranteed for every overload: it can apply to overloads handled by routing/runtime, but early gateway shedding is rejected before routing can evaluate the fallback. Recommend respecting `Retry-After` and using exponential backoff with jitter; where appropriate, discuss an alternate-region policy or capacity adjustments as mitigation. [5]

The two issues had **different causes**:

- **Activation funnel discrepancy:** The dashboard overstated US-East signups because some flows emitted duplicate signup events. Inconsistent deduplication and a region/date join that dropped some EU events further distorted the comparison; underlying warehouse events were largely correct.[3][5] The fix shipped in **PR-28521** to stop duplicate emissions, and updated the dashboard query to use consistent deduplication and remove the problematic join condition.[5]

- **Onboarding emails:** The EU-West lifecycle trigger was configured to publish to the **US-East event-bus endpoint**, causing cross-region authorization failures and preventing send requests.[1][6] The fix changed EU-West to its regional event-bus endpoint and rotated the service-token scope; eligible missed emails were then backfilled.[6]

Northpeak’s burst usage was overstated because retries—particularly client retries on 429s—could generate separate billable metering events. The stable idempotency key wasn’t consistently propagated into metering, and request IDs could change between attempts, so the existing dedupe missed duplicates. [2][3]

The fix is to generate or accept a request-scoped idempotency key at the gateway, carry it through retries and into burst usage events, and deduplicate events before billing export using tenant, region, hardware, pool, and idempotency key. A reconciliation check also blocks export and alerts if duplicate rates exceed the configured threshold. [1] The team backfilled Northpeak’s affected usage and approved an invoice adjustment. [2][3]

Compare **routing-decision logs** and **router state** in the affected region:

- **Stale config propagation:** If logs show the old configured percentage alongside the new Console target, and only some pods have the old value, check config-watch health and each pod’s last-applied config/version. In the documented incident, a watch disconnect left some us-east pods serving 25% after Console changed to 10%.[2][3][7]
- **Router version skew or cohorting behavior:** Check that routers are on the same release, and inspect cohort-key presence/source and hash inputs. A missing key with a low-entropy fallback, or an older router build using different fallback/seed behavior, can bias assignment; these are distinct from pods simply applying an old percentage.[4][5]
- **Mitigation:** For confirmed stale config, force a full config resync—typically by rolling/restarting the affected region’s router deployment—then verify the configured percentage in decision logs and that observed traffic converges. If needed for safety, pause or set that region’s canary to 0%, but don’t rely on a Console change alone when routers are stale.[2][3][4][6] For key-related skew, use a stable, high-entropy per-user or per-session key and check it is present consistently; for version skew, align router versions.[4][5]

## Reconciled contract

- **HTTP status:** `409 Conflict` for a residency-policy block, across streaming and non-streaming requests. The ADR is explicit, and the PM requirements also specify 409. [3][2]
- **Canonical SDK key:** `error.code = "residency_policy_violation"` for every residency block. SDKs should key on this stable code, not on the different initial codes listed in the PRD. [3][5][7][2]
- **Subcode:** SDKs should also inspect `error.subcode`, whose ADR-defined values are:
  - `region_not_allowed`
  - `primary_region_unavailable`
  - `policy_misconfigured` [3][5]

The PRD’s proposed codes—`RESIDENCY_POLICY_VIOLATION`, `RESIDENCY_REGION_NOT_ALLOWED`, `RESIDENCY_NO_ELIGIBLE_REGION`, and `RESIDENCY_POLICY_NOT_FOUND`—conflict with the ADR’s canonical envelope and code scheme. For the public contract, the ADR’s lowercase `error.code` plus `error.subcode` is the consistent choice. [2][3][5]

## Streaming and implementation caveat

The gateway ticket agrees on 409 and `residency_policy_violation`, but describes an SSE terminal error if a violation arrives after streaming starts. [1][8] That conflicts with the ADR, which requires enforcement before streaming bytes are written and a 409 JSON response for a blocked streaming request; it explicitly disallows an ad-hoc SSE error or generic mid-stream 500. [6] To match the ADR and PM requirement to fail early without partial streaming, the gateway should evaluate policy before committing stream headers and return the standard 409 JSON error. [2][6]

The ADR requires the `x-redwood-request-id` header and a matching `error.request_id`; the gateway ticket describes `x-request-id`. These header names are inconsistent across the sources, so the exact public header name needs confirmation; the error’s `request_id` field is required either way. [3][8]

Use **opt-in request tagging**, not tags enabled by default: strict proxies may reject the custom header before requests reach Redwood. For the documented header-based approach, let users disable tags with `REDWOOD_TEMPLATE_TELEMETRY=off`; the newer template convention enables the `X-Redwood-Template` header only when `REDWOOD_TEMPLATE_TELEMETRY=1` or `true`. [1][2][5]

When API tags are disabled, Redwood can’t derive first-tagged-request or first-success KPIs from those requests. TTFS can still use the CLI `template_init` timestamp when that event is available; otherwise it falls back to the first tagged API request, so without either source TTFS—and activation measurement requiring an init denominator—will be incomplete. [6][8]

### Classification for SLO and error budgets
- **Count a disconnect as a platform-caused failure** when Redwood terminates an active stream because of a server-side issue, such as an upstream reset or serving error, gateway timeout, routing failure, or internal error. These failures count against streaming reliability and availability; a streaming failure need not appear as an HTTP 5xx because the stream may already be established. [1][3][5][8]
- **Exclude it as a client abort** when evidence attributes the termination to the customer closing or cancelling the connection, a customer-side timeout or proxy/load-balancer termination, or a network interruption outside Redwood’s control. [1][3][8]
- **Use telemetry to attribute the cause**, including stream lifecycle/termination reason, gateway logs, request ID, timestamps, region, client error or HTTP status, SSE error events, and client/proxy timeout settings. If a reset’s initiator cannot be reliably identified, it may be conservatively counted as a stream error; the classification should be checked against the request-level evidence. [1][2]

### SLA availability and customer response
For the SLA calculation, include Redwood-attributable stream failures among failed eligible requests; exclude customer-attributable aborts and other stated exclusions. Customer-facing language should say that a streaming request is successful when it completes without a Redwood-attributed disconnect, and clearly exclude customer client, proxy, and network terminations. [3][8]

Support should explain that not every mid-stream disconnect is a 5xx, describe the attribution rule and uncertainty for ambiguous resets, and ask for request IDs and timestamps to investigate. It can recommend reviewing proxy idle timeouts, ensuring the client continues reading, and setting suitable stream-duration or output limits. [1][2]

## V1 streaming standard
- Enforce an **overall wall-clock timeout** even if the underlying client cannot provide one, plus a streaming **idle timeout** that resets when bytes/events arrive. The standard gives 90 seconds overall and 30 seconds idle; the parity matrix also calls for connect/first-byte timeout handling. [1][6]
- **Do not automatically retry after any partial output**; surface a typed streaming-disconnect error with request ID and partial-output/attempt details. A retry may be allowed before the first byte/event if the failure is retryable and budget remains. [1][3]

## SDKs and known issues
- **Python:** A support ticket documented streaming reads hanging because timeouts were not applied in the read loop. The proposed fix was to honor overall timeout/cancellation and return a typed error, but the supplied sources do not confirm the fix shipped. [2]
- **TypeScript:** A ticket reported retries on HTTP 400. The mitigation was to restrict retry classification, and later refactor notes say 400-class responses are no longer retried (except 429); the sources do not establish release status. [2][5]
- **Go:** A ticket documented missing `Retry-After` handling on 429, causing rapid retries. This is a retry-standard violation, but the sources do not confirm the fix shipped. [2]

**Bottom line:** The sources document real Python streaming-timeout and TS/Go retry issues, but do not provide a complete current-status matrix showing whether they remain in released SDKs. [2][5][6]

### Causes

- **Request-log TTL issue:** The 7-day policy was configured correctly, with no legal or incident hold active. A telemetry database maintenance window caused slower deletion and repeated purge-job timeouts; throttling and retries built up a backlog in us-east, leaving records older than the configured TTL temporarily present. [7][8]
- **Audit-export issue:** The exporter’s report template used an event-type allowlist that likely lagged newer event types or omitted RBAC and API-key categories. As a result, the export missed events that were visible in the Console or internal queries; the exact taxonomy scope for `console.login` was still unclear. [6]

Do not imply real-time deletion or a strict per-hour guarantee. [2][4][7][8]

## SLO targets and abort criteria

- **Fast tier:** p99 must be **≤700 ms for short prompts**; streaming TTFT p99 must be **≤450 ms** in hosted US/EU. [2]
- **Hard abort:** Roll back if fast-tier p99 stays above **115% of its SLO target OR 120% of baseline for 10 minutes**. [3] The initial canary guidance also calls for immediate rollback if fast-tier p99 exceeds **115% of target for 10 minutes** in a canary region for a top model. [2]
- The perf-canary gate separately requires streaming TTFT p99 and non-streaming p99 not to regress by more than **7% from baseline**, while remaining under their absolute targets. [1]
- If fast-tier TTFT p99 regresses by more than **10% for 15 minutes**, pause the ramp and investigate. [2] A fast-tier p99 abort is a paging condition. [3]

## Rollback steps

1. Set `tiered_batching_defaults_enabled=false` globally. [3]
2. Verify propagation on the control-plane status page; it should take less than two minutes. [3]
3. Confirm `reason_code=TIER_DEFAULT` drops to about zero in canary regions. [3]
4. If latency has not recovered within 10 minutes, restore `scheduler.max_wait_ms` to the legacy default via emergency override. [3]
5. If customers are affected, post in `#incidents`, then summarize in `#eng-sre`. If p99 has not recovered within 15 minutes after rollback, treat it as a separate incident and keep defaults off until the release candidate. [3]

## Dashboards and reason codes for diagnosis

Use the **Tiered Batching — Latency & Streaming** dashboard for p99 and TTFT split by tier and streaming mode, and **Tiered Batching — Queue & Backpressure** for queue depth, wait time, admission rejects, shed counts, and overload-mode status. [7] Also inspect batch-formation metrics such as `max_wait_ms` utilization and prefill/decode occupancy, alongside queue depth and admission rejects. [7][2]

Check reason-code counts over time to verify which profile is active and why. [4] For admission-control or overload behavior, look for `tier.overload_mode.active`; the scheduler also emits `overload_admission_block` and `overload_shed` when admission is blocked or requests are shed. [4][6] To investigate unexpected tier selection, check `tier.default.fast|standard|cost_efficient`, `tier.override.route_policy`, `tier.constrained.model_limit`, and `tier.fallback.compat_variant`. [4] For requeue/wait-budget behavior specifically, the sources describe tracing spans and structured reason codes when the wait budget triggers or starvation prevention forces eligibility, but do not give their exact reason-code names. [6]

### Check first
Treat a non-burst neighbor latency complaint as high priority. Check the SLO regression gate and any automated burst reduction, correlate tail-latency changes with the burst window, and involve SRE. Also verify the tenant remains pinned to Dedicated capacity, then inspect burst-pool utilization, router queue depth, and admission-controller latency/errors; the incident evidence shows shared routing dependencies can affect non-burst traffic even when it never uses burst GPUs. [1][6][7]

### When to reduce caps or stop burst
- **Reduce caps:** Use a cap reduction as an immediate mitigation when saturation or suspected neighbor impact appears. The incident team reduced the regional burst safety cap and paused the offending tenant’s burst. [1][7] The operational policy also calls for reducing burst caps by 50% when the non-burst latency guardrail persists beyond 30 minutes. [5]
- **SLO gate:** This is the automated response to sustained non-burst latency regression: it can first reduce the effective burst ratio, then disable new burst permits if regression crosses a higher threshold or persists. The documented defaults are a 3-minute entry window for reduction and a 10-minute disable threshold, with recovery required before the gate exits. [4]
- **Circuit breaker:** Open it when fleet safety triggers warrant denying burst—such as pool saturation, stale telemetry, or a non-burst SLO regression gate. It is the hard-stop mechanism for new burst admissions; the SLO gate complements the pool-saturation breaker by directly protecting non-burst latency. [2][4][8]

### Denial reason
When the SLO gate disables burst, the documented reason is `SLO_GATED`. A fleet-safety circuit-breaker denial uses `FLEET_SAFETY_CIRCUIT_OPEN`. [2][4]

### Escalation and status page
- Use a Support bridge for customer-specific triage, but move to **#incidents** if there is suspected multi-customer or multi-region impact, service-degradation-level errors or latency, production-wide mitigation/rollback, an anticipated status page update, or a need for formal incident roles. The bridge lead should announce the reason, hand off context, and link the incident channel in SUP-1842. [8]
- A status page incident is an immediate “yes” for confirmed platform symptoms affecting two or more customers, critical-tier impact with expected SLA concerns, or externally noticeable regional/product degradation. It is usually warranted if impact persists beyond 15 minutes without quick mitigation or traffic shifts/fallbacks are underway. A single-customer configuration issue generally does not warrant one. [5]
- In the SUP-1842 discussion, Redwood had internal incident tracking but did not commit to a status page post because the issue was streaming-specific, not a full region outage; they would reconsider if impact expanded or broader impact became clear. [3][4]

- Send email updates **every 60 minutes while impact persists**, and within **30 minutes of a material change**; once stabilized, move to **twice daily** until fully resolved and postmortem. Keep updates customer-safe and avoid speculation. [2][3]
- Keep email and SUP-1842 as the customer-facing system of record rather than splitting context into a real-time Slack Connect backchannel. [3][4]

### Mitigations applied
- Disabled kernel auto-selection v2 for the affected Llama models on Northwind’s dedicated L40S pool, `nw-analytics-ded-01` in us-east, and added a temporary deny rule blocking `fa3_fused_prefill_sm89` for LONG requests on L40S.[2][3]
- The mitigation restored p99 latency to roughly 5.3–5.8 seconds for 18–22k-token prompts, near the pre-canary baseline; no new errors or correctness regressions were observed.[1][3]

### Safe re-enable plan and criteria
- Keep the deny in place through Runtime 1.21 GA. Re-enable v2 only after the fix is included in Runtime 1.21.1, L40S long-context benchmarks are green, and a controlled canary is run on Northwind’s pool.[1][5]
- Run the canary with dashboards and an explicit rollback window; roll back if LONG-bucket p99 regresses by more than 10%.[1][5]
- The fix is intended to correct LONG-bucket classification and add an L40S-specific penalty for the underperforming prefill kernel. The sources recommend keeping the deny in place for driver 550.54.14 until validation is complete.[1][3]

### Why the header was missing
The gateway added `Retry-After` when its own admission control shed a request, but did not consistently add it when a downstream runtime or routing service returned an overload error. Those responses could pass through with an overload body but no header, explaining why some 503s lacked it while gateway-generated 429s had it. [1][5]

### Changes to improve consistency
- The gateway now applies or preserves `Retry-After` for mapped overload errors regardless of whether they originate at the gateway or downstream; it avoids adding the header to generic, non-overload 5xx errors. [1][2][3]
- The shared overload-response handling standardizes the header as integer seconds and includes correlation/request IDs. Routing errors retain their code and message while receiving normalized headers. [2][3]
- For streaming, overload rejection is performed before the response starts, so the gateway can send the header; after headers have been committed, it cannot reliably add one. [2][3]
- The gateway has tests for overload header presence and formatting, downstream propagation, streaming rejection before stream start, and protection against setting the header on generic 5xx responses. [2][3]

### Monitoring and alerts
A missing-header counter and logging were added as a canary check, intended to remain at zero. [2] The rollout also calls for monitoring Retry-After presence, overload shed rates, and related error metrics; a separate reliability discussion proposes investigating regional shed rates at 0.2%, paging at 0.5%, and rolling back if shedding exceeds 1% during canary. [2][7][8]

### Why the percentages diverged
In the reported us-east incident, a config-watch stream disconnected and some router pods did not reconnect. Those pods kept serving the last-applied rollout configuration of **25%**, even though the Console/control plane had updated the step to **10%**. Other pods had the new config, producing a region-level split mismatch. [2][3][8]

### Recommended oncall mitigations
- Check router config-watch health and the last-applied rollout version/age; investigate watch errors or lag in the affected region. [1][4]
- If routers are using stale config, roll or restart the router deployment to force a fresh config pull, then verify decision logs and wait for regional traffic metrics to converge. [2][4][8]
- If production risk warrants it, freeze or pause the rollout; however, a Console change may not take effect on pods still using stale config, so ensure router resync completes. [3][4][8]

### GA preventative fixes
- Add periodic full config resync and a watch-health watchdog, with alerts for watch connectivity and stale config age. [2][8]
- For GA, validate idempotent control-plane-to-data-plane propagation and verify per-region split accuracy within **±2 percentage points over a 15-minute window** for stable-volume traffic. [5]

### SDK examples and fixtures

Use the actual `event.type` strings in code, not friendly aliases. The shared streaming sequence includes `response.started`, `response.output_text.delta`, `response.tool_call.delta`, and `response.completed`; `response.output_text.completed`, `response.tool_call.completed`, and `response.failed` are also named, but `response.tool_call.completed` may not appear for every model. Treat `response.completed` as authoritative when it includes final state. [1]

For assembly, accumulate assistant text and tool calls by ID, merging fragmented tool-argument deltas; do not parse arguments until the call is complete. Golden fixtures should cover fragmented arguments and verify ordering and final assembled tool-call arguments. [1][3][7]

### OpenAI-compat mapping

Map OpenAI function-call argument tokens incrementally into Redwood `response.tool_call.delta` events, preserving their order and enough information to reconstruct the final call. Assemble the arguments, then invoke the tool only after finalization; map the finalized name and arguments into the canonical tool-call state. [2][4]

The sources describe both `response.tool_call.completed` and finalization via `response.completed`, but say the former is not guaranteed. Therefore, examples should merge deltas and use the completed response’s final snapshot when available, rather than requiring a separate tool-call-completed event. [1]

## Canonical contract

A residency-policy block returns **HTTP 409 Conflict** with the standard Redwood `error` envelope. Its stable code is `residency_policy_violation`; the error includes a human-readable message, a stable subcode, a matching `request_id` and `x-redwood-request-id`, a `help_url`, and bounded diagnostic details such as allowed regions, candidate region, and policy scope. [1]

For streaming requests, the gateway should evaluate residency **before committing streaming headers**: a pre-stream block returns the same 409 JSON response without starting SSE. If a structured violation arrives after streaming starts, the gateway emits an SSE `error` event containing the serialized error payload, then closes the connection. [2]

## Where it is enforced

- **Gateway:** A shared middleware/error mapper translates routing or policy-engine violations into the standardized payload across chat, completions, and legacy aliases. The required order is authentication, policy evaluation, then response-mode selection. [2] The implementation also describes centralized serialization in `gateway/errors/public_errors.ts`, including REST and streaming adapters. [8]
- **Python SDK:** The SDK maps a 409 residency-enforcement error to `ResidencyPolicyViolationError`, a subclass of `APIError`. It exposes the error code, request ID, and help URL; other errors retain existing handling. For streaming, it raises this exception when the initial response is an error; mid-stream transport failures are unchanged. [7]

The sources differ on some public error field names and codes; the ADR’s `residency_policy_violation` code and required envelope fields are the canonical contract. [1]

### Expected workflow

1. **Keep `unknown` provisional.** Use `incident_type = unknown` and `subtype = unknown` only when there is active impact or credible risk and evidence cannot distinguish between multiple top-level types without guessing. Assign **SRE (Reliability) as the temporary primary owner**. Record what is known and unknown, the next 1–3 steps to clarify, and when classification will be revisited in the incident channel. [1][6]

2. **Revisit promptly.** Sev0/Sev1 classification is required within **10 minutes** of incident declaration or incident-bot creation, whichever is earlier. For an incident that remains unknown, revisit at **T+30 minutes and T+60 minutes from incident start**; if still unknown at the second checkpoint, ask the SRE Duty Manager to arbitrate. When evidence supports a category, update the type/subtype and post a brief reclassification note; if the owner changes, engage the new owner’s on-call immediately. [1][6][7]

3. **SLA clock and alerts while unknown.** The SLA clock starts when the incident is declared in incident-bot and severity is set. Unknown classification gets a **15-minute grace period** for Sev0/Sev1; after that, the incident uses the conservative/default SLA targets for its tier and severity until its type is updated. TTM stops at **Mitigated** and TTF at **Resolved**. Sev0/Sev1 mitigation warnings are scheduled for 30 and 10 minutes before the target, and applicable fix warnings for 60 minutes before the target; breaches generate Slack alerts and, under the stated paging rules, page the primary owner and SRE for Sev0 breaches, or page SRE and notify the primary-owner channel for Sev1 breaches. [2][3][4]

The sources specify the 15-minute SLA grace period separately from the classification policy’s 10-minute requirement; they do not explain how to reconcile those two timing thresholds. [2][7]

### Recommended starting configuration
- Use **`mode=drain`**—not panic—and enable the watchdog only for the bounded Dedicated canary slice. The proposed initial timeouts are **2,000 ms for collectives** and **5,000 ms for decode**; these are tentative and should be validated against perf-canary data. [1]
- Keep the watchdog **off by default in production**, enabling it explicitly for the canary. [1][4]

### Immediate rollback conditions
- **Disable the watchdog promptly** if false positives cause **more than 3 drain/restart events per hour per cluster without a corresponding reduction in request timeouts**. [2]
- Treat **widespread watchdog-triggered drains** as an immediate stop condition; the canary plan also calls for rollback if drains occur without recovery or replicas wedge for more than 10 minutes. [2][7]
- Other hard-stop signals include a **customer-visible 5xx or timeout increase above 0.5% absolute over 60 minutes**, attributable to runtime behavior, or a **sustained p99 regression above 10% for more than 2 hours**. [2]

A quality-regression block is a targeted policy constraint for the specific model, variant, and profile. The policy engine returns a distinct **blocked** outcome, records it separately in metrics and the audit trail, and deterministically resolves the route to baseline precision—even if the route configuration still references that profile. An incompatibility is a separate fallback outcome; the hotfix explicitly distinguishes `blocked` from `incompatible` so they can be observed and alerted on separately. [1]

To verify a customer route is back on baseline, oncall should:

- **Check logs:** Confirm the route’s request logs show the profile resolution outcome. For a blocked profile, look for `quant_profile_resolution=blocked` and the resolved baseline; for a disabled profile, verify the profile is marked disabled or absent. [1][2][3]
- **Check dashboards:** Confirm fallback-rate and latency signals have returned to normal, and review the relevant metrics for the route. [2][3]
- **Check audit history:** Review the Console change history for the route-setting change and its actor; the checklist also calls for confirming the audit/change-history diff. [2][3]

The docs say route-level rollback typically takes effect within a few minutes and recommend verifying via logs. [2]

### Recommended remediation
The retention policy was configured correctly; the issue was a purge backlog after telemetry database maintenance slowed deletions and automatic throttling reduced purge throughput. Verify the policy and confirm there are no legal-hold or other exceptions, run a controlled backfill purge through the current 7-day cutoff, and temporarily raise purge-worker concurrency with database-pressure guardrails. Monitor purge failures and `ttl_lag_seconds` until lag is back within the normal range (under 6 hours). [1][2]

### Customer-safe evidence
Provide:
- A retention configuration export showing the 7-day request-log TTL and its scope, with no legal hold enabled. [1][3][5]
- A redacted dashboard screenshot or metric showing `ttl_lag_seconds` returning to normal; the customer was sent this along with the config export. [1]
- A short written confirmation that, as of March 13, 2025, request/response logs older than seven days were no longer queryable in us-east and the backlog had been cleared. [1][3]

### Fastest recovery during the call
- **Stop load-generating scenarios:** pause live load tests and use single-request scenarios; reduce parallelism. If 429s persist, pause synthetic traffic and retry after the 60-second rate-limit window resets. [2][4][5]
- **Switch to backup content immediately:** use screenshots or a short recording, then continue with the reliability narrative and Q&A. Don’t spend the live call debugging or repeatedly retrying. [1][2]
- **For empty dashboards:** check the selected project and time range; if needed, start the synthetic traffic generator. If the graphs still don’t populate quickly, use the prepared screenshots and keep narrating. [1][2][4]

### Prevention fixes
- Demo quotas were raised and provisioning was updated to apply the demo quota profile reliably; a healthcheck now verifies quota and rate-limit settings before demos. [5][8]
- Synthetic traffic was separated from live demos into a dedicated seed project/key, with separate scoped keys for live-demo and seed traffic. [5][8]
- Dashboard defaults were improved to select the seeded demo project and a sensible time range, and the empty state still flags when no events have arrived. [3][7]

## Current suppression rules

- **Intent-only signals cannot create HubSpot tasks** unless there is an explicit request or a qualifying combined signal—intent plus a threshold signal such as spend, tokens, repeated 429s, or team expansion. The shipped pilot rule also requires confidence of at least **0.85** for intent signals. [5][6]
- Additional Quartz-specific gates require baseline activity or an explicit inbound request; intent must appear on at least **two different days within seven days**; and a nurture email in the prior **five days** suppresses an AE task unless a usage threshold is met. A DNC flag blocks automated task creation and timeline notes for at least **90 days**. [7]
- More generally, routing requires the score cutoff, confidence of at least **0.70** by default, and a non-vanity high-intent action; pricing-page or docs-homepage views alone do not qualify. Scale signals must meet sustained-usage criteria rather than being a one-day spike. [1][4]
- Internal/test organizations are blocked unless explicitly allowlisted. Suppressed candidates are recorded internally for analysis rather than routed to HubSpot. [1][4]

## Cooldowns and task suppression

- The MVP specifies a per-organization, per-signal cooldown of **14 days by default**, **7 days** for reliability signals, and **21 days** for compliance-intent signals. An open router task within that period prevents another task; the router instead updates company properties and adds a timeline note. [1][4]
- The routing ADR gives a different set of task cooldowns: **7 days** for reliability, **14 days** for scale, and **30 days** for security/compliance intent. It also blocks a new task when a PLG task is open and was created within **14 days**. [3]
- After a false-positive disposition, the Quartz update says re-notification is suppressed for **30 days**. Quartz itself was also marked Do Not Contact and excluded from the pilot. [6]

These layers prevent another task by filtering weak or vanity intent, requiring corroborating evidence or an explicit request, honoring DNC and other suppression flags, and suppressing duplicate or recently open tasks. [1][3][6][7] The sources describe differing cooldown schedules (notably 21 versus 30 days for compliance intent); they do not establish which schedule supersedes the other. [1][3]

### Recovery path
1. Treat a control-plane outage lasting over 10 minutes, or migration lock contention beyond thresholds, as a stop condition: escalate to Private SRE and Release Engineering and update the customer as required. [2]
2. Inspect the migration-job and Postgres logs, and identify long-running transactions in `pg_stat_activity`. Scale down control-plane deployments to release old connections; if the migration remains blocked, terminate the blocking Postgres backend, then rerun the failed migration job. Restarting Postgres was suggested if scaling down did not clear the issue. [5][6]
3. Once migrations complete, bring the control plane back up and verify deployment readiness, that pods are not crash-looping, and that version endpoints report the target version. [1][5]
4. If rollback is needed, use only the supported rollback tooling, which uses stored upgrade state for deterministic reversal, runs hooks in order, and checks control- and data-plane health. Attach the rollback report and final status to the change record. [2] The incident materials describe a rollback command as future work, so they do not establish that this tooling is available in every deployment. [1]

### Change-management evidence
Retain the upgrade plan and human summary; precheck and backup reports (including backup identifiers); upgrade execution report or state-machine logs; installer logs and artifact manifests; and a rollback report if rollback is used. Keep audit events for upgrade start, precheck pass/fail, backup completion, upgrade completion/failure, and rollback invocation/completion. [2]

For traceability, the plan should identify the environment, versions, stages, and rollback entry points; execution records should capture step results and state; and audit events should include timestamps, actor, environment/cluster, versions, plan ID, outcome, and failure reason when applicable. Support bundles should include the plan, execution state/logs, prechecks, rollback state if present, installer version/build, Helm history, and relevant Kubernetes events, with secrets redacted. [3] The change record should include final status, duration, deviations, and incident links or lessons learned where applicable. [2]

For opt-in KPI tracking, the quickstart specification standardizes on four headers: `X-Redwood-Template-Id`, `X-Redwood-Template-Version`, `X-Redwood-Template-Lang`, and `X-Redwood-Template-Install-Id` (a random UUID; do not use it as a metric dimension). [4] An earlier proposal describes a single `x-redwood-template-tags` header with semicolon-separated key/value pairs, but the later specification gives the four-header convention. [1][4]

Telemetry is disabled by default, so templates don’t send those headers unless users explicitly enable it. [3][4] If a corporate proxy blocks the headers, users should disable tagging; templates should continue working without it. [3][4]

The oscillation was attributed to noisy regional impairment signals combined with insufficient rollback/anti-flap guardrails. In particular, reachability probes recovered for some edges while 5xx burn remained elevated, and inconsistent corroboration let rollback logic classify a policy as recovered too early; hold-down/anti-flap interplay contributed to an unexpected rollback. [2][3][7]

The streaming reconnect fix was tracked as **ENG-2422** (related support ticket **SUP-25322**), with a target to ship to production behind a feature flag by **2026-02-07**. [2]

The root cause was a deduplication bug in the usage exporter: retried streaming chunks were counted as separate completions when the request ID changed across retry boundaries. The hosted API and invoices were unaffected; invoice generation used a separate validated counter. [1]

As mitigation, export generation was paused, then the affected data was backfilled after the fix; corrected exports resumed at 22:10 UTC. [1] Follow-ups were to add a daily, per-workspace reconciliation between invoice and export counters, alert on drift above 0.5%, fix deduplication to use a stable trace ID across retries, and add a contract test for streaming-retry behavior. [1]

The AD connector began emitting a leading UTF-8 BOM (`EF BB BF` / U+FEFF) before the first group in the comma-separated `groups` attribute. The parser split the string and trimmed whitespace, but did not remove the BOM, so the first value remained BOM-prefixed and failed the exact-match check for `crestline-admins`; SAML login succeeded, but the expected admin role was not mapped. [1][2]

The server-side fix added SAML attribute normalization to strip BOM and other common invisible characters before trimming and role mapping. Patch v1.14.3 was deployed to the private control plane and restored the affected users’ admin roles. [2][3]

Tune these first:

1. **Reduce `kv.compaction.budget_ms_per_step`**—the per-step time budget. Make a conservative reduction; the sources give no specific amount or recommended decrement. [2][5]
2. **Increase `kv.compaction.fragmentation_trigger_ratio` slightly**—so compaction starts less often. The sources likewise don’t specify an exact increase. [2][5]

For an immediate disable, set the impacted pool’s **`kv.compaction.kill_switch=true`**; the kill-switch takes priority over the enabled setting. [2][3][5] Then confirm the effective config via `kv_compaction_config_kill_switch` (1) and check that `runtime_kv_compaction_steps_total` stops increasing; bytes moved should drop to roughly zero, and compaction spans should disappear. [2][3][7] The disable may wait for an in-flight move to reach a safe point, so check `kv_compaction_disable_inflight_moves_total` and `kv_compaction_disable_wait_ms` as well. [3]

The storm was an alerting failure, not a confirmed customer latency regression. After coverage expanded from 3 to 8 models and paging was enabled, baseline lookup keys no longer matched consistently, so some evaluations fell back to default thresholds. At the same time, high-cardinality metric labels fragmented time series, undermining sample-size checks; alert grouping differed from evaluator grouping, and incident-bot dedupe lacked stable dimensions, producing repeated pages and threads. [1][2][3]

To stop the noise, the team disabled paging while retaining warnings, rolled coverage back to the stable 3-model configuration, pinned evaluation to fixed baseline artifacts, and dropped high-cardinality labels such as `workload_run_id`, `prompt_template_id`, and full `route`. [2][3] Later fixes normalized baseline keys, treated a missing baseline as a canary-health warning rather than applying default regression thresholds, aligned alert grouping and sample/dampening requirements with the evaluator, and expanded the dedupe key to include model, version, region, hardware SKU, runtime build, and alert type. [2]

The underlying cause was an autoscaler PromQL refactor that changed label matching from `cluster_id` to `cluster`; clusters that emitted only `cluster_id` then produced empty query results, preventing scale decisions. [1]

The hotfix restored label compatibility and added a fallback query for cases where no series were returned, after which scale-out resumed. [1]

The identity-proxy cached role assertions by SAML `session_index`. After the IdP group sync, already-logged-in users’ sessions could keep returning the old role set until the cache expired, causing stale RBAC decisions and intermittent 403s. Logging out and back in refreshed the session and restored access. [1][8]

**Mitigation:** We lowered the session-cache TTL to 5 seconds during the sync window and revoked sessions for affected admins. [5][8]  
**Long-term fix:** We added and enabled server-side cache eviction when identity-change webhooks arrive, so affected cached roles are invalidated after group changes. [5][8]

The root cause was a race in the SSE gateway: after an upstream TCP reset, an in-flight terminal-event flush could interleave with a scheduled heartbeat, causing the terminal `end` event to be dropped—especially when the client resumed immediately. [2]

The server-side fix (PR 2147) made terminal-event emission atomic, ordered heartbeats after the terminal flush, and added a 250 ms resume grace window so the gateway could observe socket teardown before accepting a resume. [2]

The reset was caused by a frontend regression: the widget editor’s post-save handler, changed in PR 4521, dispatched a global `presets:clear` event after a successful sub-report save. That cleared the dashboard’s preset state in the Redux store; traces found no server-side preset-change call. [2][3]

The hotfix scoped post-save events to the editor’s local state, preventing the modal save from dispatching `presets:clear` globally. Staging tests confirmed presets stayed selected after editing and saving a linked sub-report. [3][5]

**Mitigations applied:** SRE/Ops increased proxy replicas and redistributed traffic, then widened the affected nodes’ ephemeral port range from the default `32768–60999` to `10240–65535` using a temporary sysctl change. The customer was also asked to reduce concurrent streaming traffic. These actions brought errors back to baseline. [1][3][6]

**RCA artifacts to capture while the issue is ongoing (playbook):**
- A 90-second `tcpdump` capture from an affected proxy, uploaded to incident artifact storage. [4]
- 25% trace sampling on the impacted route for two hours. [4]
- Metrics covering 30 minutes before the incident, during it, and two hours after. [5]
- The affected-tenant list, with exact error counts and timestamps. [5]

The trigger was a 01:55 UTC edge-config change that reduced upstream keepalive/connection TTL from 90 seconds to 10 seconds, increasing connection churn during a traffic burst and exposing a streaming-proxy write-stall bug. The stalled writes left buffers frozen while the proxy continued accepting streaming data, causing head-of-line stalls and backlog growth.[7][8]

Immediate mitigations were to restart the affected streaming-proxy fleet, roll back the TTL change to 90 seconds, and apply temporary traffic shaping: a soft concurrency limit per upstream instance and rejection of new sessions on overloaded proxies.[7][8]

The edge-proxy canary rewrote the cookie domain to `.redwood.ai`, while some long-poll clients continued sending the original host-scoped cookie. The session-manager treated that domain mismatch as an unauthenticated session during pin reconciliation, dropped the pinned routing key, and sent requests down the fallback path. [1][3]

**Immediate mitigations:**
- **Platform-side:** Rolled back/disabled the cookie-domain rewrite for the us-east canary cohort. [4][5]
- **Customer-side:** Advised BrightChat to force a session refresh (`POST /v1/sessions/refresh`); refreshed sessions saw pinned routing restored. [3][6]

**Confirmed root cause:** The catalog migration/promotion failed to persist LexicoHealth’s tenant-specific alias override, so `open-embed-default` unexpectedly resolved to the 1024-d model instead of the 512-d model expected by its stored vectors and reranker. The reranker strictly validates vector dimensions and does not automatically convert mixed dimensions. [1][2][5]

**Mitigation and fix:** Short term, the team applied a routing override to `open-embed-512-v1`, restored the tenant alias, and helped the customer pin the model and restart workers. [3][5] The permanent catalog fix was a hotfix to preserve tenant alias mappings; longer-term prevention work under INT-1123 included a backward-compatible reranker adapter and catalog validation to catch alias drift. [2][5]

For an allowed break-glass session, emit the applicable **read event**—`incident_bot.config_diff.read` for a config diff and/or `incident_bot.telemetry.query` for a privileged telemetry query—plus `incident_bot.break_glass.activate` when the elevation is granted and `incident_bot.break_glass.deactivate` when it expires or is revoked. [1][3] Privileged calls made under break-glass must also include `break_glass=true` and the session ID. [3]

Retention for incident-bot privileged access events is **400 days searchable in the SIEM** and **7 years in immutable archive**. [2]

The permission scopes are:

| Read | Baseline scope | Break-glass scope |
|---|---|---|
| Config diff | `config.read:diff_redacted` | `config.read:diff_expanded_redacted` |
| Telemetry | `telemetry.read:diagnostics_templates` | `telemetry.read:tenant_scoped` |

Break-glass scopes are restricted to eligible Sev0/Sev1 incidents and are time-limited. [5]

**Root cause:** The gateway signed the payload *after compression*. The retry used a different encoding/compression path, and proxy decompression or re-serialization could also alter the raw bytes. So, although the logical JSON stayed the same, the bytes being signed differed and the HMAC signature changed. [1][3]

**Planned server-side fix:** Sign a canonical representation of the logical payload *before compression*, so retries with different transport encodings produce verifiable signatures. The fix was planned for a staged canary rollout, followed by full rollout. [2]

The rotation exposed two incomplete migrations: some Console pods still read stale legacy cache entries keyed by the old `api_key_id`, and historical usage-index records retained that old key metadata, so trace links could point to traces the new key could not resolve. [1][4][8]

As an immediate mitigation, Support/SRE flushed BrightHealth AI’s legacy cache entries and enabled the `ff/console/rotation-cache-bypass` flag, making affected queries read the live index after a recent rotation. A `?bust=1` query parameter was also offered to bypass the Console cache. [3][5][7]

- **Fallback trigger and exclusions:** In the March 3 incident, fallback was enabled when saturation exceeded **90%** or the **503 rate exceeded 0.5%**. It applied only where customer policy allowed cross-region; routes marked **`data_residency_strict`** were excluded. [1]
- **Customer content under region pinning:** This includes prompts, messages and other input text; customer-provided tool/function arguments; uploaded or retrieved documents; model outputs, including streaming tokens; embeddings inputs and vectors derived from customer text; rerank inputs and outputs; and content-bearing debug payloads or derived artifacts that could reconstruct content, such as token logs or decoded segments. Such content must remain in allowed regions. [2]

The evaluator coerced an absent `entitlements` claim into a single empty-string value. The `not_in` membership check then found no match and evaluated the exclusion expression as true, allowing the request. [1][3]

**Immediate workaround:** Set `entitlements` to an empty array for affected service accounts and short-lived tokens; as a policy-side mitigation, explicitly check `exists(user.entitlements)` and deny when the claim is absent. [1]

**Server-side fix and rollout:** AuthZ prepared a fix to stop coercing absent claims to an empty string and handle them as an empty set in `not_in`. The plan was a staging canary on **2026-03-15**, followed by a hosted release and a private-control-plane patch bundle on **2026-03-18**. [1]

The fallback policy’s `preferred_variant` was set to `"latest"` instead of `"stable-quantized"`, so fallback traffic looped back to the failing canary rather than the stable variant [2].

The team paused the rollout, changed fallback to force `stable-quantized`, drained the canary pods in eu-west-1, and lowered the sticky TTL [2]. After the policy change, 5xx errors fell from 18% to 1.2% over three minutes [2].

Each shadow probe telemetry record in a private deployment must include: `probe_id`, `tenant_id` (hashed or obfuscated), `deployed_model`, `deployment_variant`, `quant_profile`, `hardware_tag`, `prompt_family`, `seed_context_hash`, `latency_ms`, `tokens_input`, `tokens_generated`, `top_level_metrics`, `error_code`, and `timestamp_utc`. [1]

The evaluator must emit the run-lifecycle events `eval.run.start` (with `run_id`, `plugin_name`, `slice_id`, and `mode`), `eval.run.progress` (with `run_id`, `percent`, and `sampled_latency_ms`), and `eval.run.complete` (with `run_id`, `result_counts`, and `summary_metrics`). [2]

The failures had two related causes: the key-rotation sync service mishandled a chunked keyserver response and truncated public-key exports, leaving some runners with malformed or stale key material; differing GPG versions across signing hosts and runner images also caused inconsistent import and signature verification. The signer used key `ABCD1234`, while the published key was `EFGH5678`.[2][6][7]

To unblock hotfix promotions, operations temporarily rolled the signing host back to the previous key and added that key to a temporary allowlist on three runners. They force-refreshed those runners’ keyrings and verified a hotfix candidate passed. The broader keyring rollout, keysync patch with checksum validation, and GPG-version standardization were left as permanent follow-up work.[2][6]

### Underlying cause
A stale, long-running Postgres session from a previous failed attempt was holding the advisory lock, so the migration runner kept waiting. The database being externally managed does not change the indicated cause: the lock was in Postgres, and the DBA identified the session there. [1][2][5]

### Action that resolved it
Support advised holding off on canceling or retrying until evidence was collected. The customer’s DBA found and terminated the stale lock-holding session; migrations then progressed and the upgrade completed about 10 minutes later. [1][2]

### Collect before retry or rollback
- Installer logs and migration-runner stdout/stderr, including output from the start of the migration step and timestamps for when the upgrade started and appeared stuck. [1][6]
- Migration pod/job details: `kubectl describe` and logs, plus relevant cluster events and pod status. [6]
- Current and target control-plane versions and installer version. [6]
- A DBA-provided snapshot of active Postgres sessions and locks during the migration window; high-level Postgres connectivity/health information is also requested. [1][2][6]

Only consider a controlled retry after collecting logs and confirming there is no partial schema corruption. Rollback should wait until it is confirmed that no irreversible migrations have run; do not perform manual schema downgrades without Platform approval. [6][8]

The Hosted API fix chose a resume identifier formatted as `v1:{stream_id}:{flush_offset}:{crc8}`, base64-encoded for compactness in headers [1]. The checkpointing standard sets the default cadence at every **512 tokens or 10 seconds, whichever comes first**, and the default checkpoint TTL at **24 hours** [2][3].

Set the request header `X-Redwood-Cache-Policy: force-bypass` to prevent cache reads and writes [2]. For `interactive-chat`, the policy requires at least a 60% KV-cache hit rate and limits quantized requests to a maximum sequence length of 2048 tokens [1].

The added header is `x-redwood-fallback-reason` [1][2]. The sources do not specify a standardized per-fallback telemetry event envelope or the fields required in it. They describe normalization outputs such as `normalized_unit`, `normalized_cost`, `normalization_version`, and `normalization_flags`, but do not identify these as required fields for a per-fallback event envelope [5].

The span ingester’s queue had a low maximum size and dropped spans when full. A parallel deploy added attributes, increasing spans per request and pushing the queue into frequent drops under burst load. [1]

The immediate mitigation was to increase ingester replicas and temporarily raise queue limits; the drop rate returned to baseline as the backlog drained. [1]

Duplicate executions occurred because retries sometimes reached the service with different byte representations of the same logical idempotency key. SDKs differed in Unicode normalization (Python sent NFD; Go sent NFC), and the edge proxy could percent-encode or fold non-ASCII header values during HTTP/2 handling. The server compared the raw keys, treated the mismatched bytes as distinct, and executed the tool/webhook again. This was associated with non-ASCII keys passing through HTTP/2 and the edge; plain ASCII keys did not show the discrepancy. [1][2][3][7]

The recommended workaround was to encode keys as ASCII-safe base64 or hex (or avoid non-ASCII keys); the customer reported no duplicate events during a 24-hour check after switching to base64. [3][5][6] The server-side fix was to canonicalize incoming keys to UTF-8 NFC before storage and lookup, with a follow-up plan to make lookups tolerant of existing stored keys by normalizing both stored and incoming values. ## Emergency rollback procedure

1. **Confirm the decision and owners.** The Incident Commander owns the rollback decision; Runtime oncall validates the cause and target, and Release/Infra oncall executes the change. Declare an incident if customer impact is confirmed or likely, and identify a prior release known to be good (at least 24 hours stable in production). [1][4]

2. **Record the rollback details** in the incident channel: current and target release tags, affected Hosted regions and Dedicated clusters/tenants, and the main symptom. [1][4]

3. **Stop the rollout.** Pause any in-flight progressive rollout and prevent automation from advancing it again. [1][2]

4. **Roll back Hosted fleets.** Pin the Hosted runtime to the target tag and redeploy. Roll back any canary-only non-critical region first, then the remaining canary cohort, then all regions on the bad release. After each region, check that errors, GPU utilization, TTFT, and tokens per second recover. Lock the tag if auto-advance could reintroduce the bad release. [1][2]

5. **Roll back Dedicated clusters.** Use the Dedicated Runtime Release Adoption dashboard to identify affected clusters and confirm which are on the bad release. Pin the target tag and redeploy each affected cluster. Consider customer change windows; for sensitive tenants, coordinate with Customer Success according to the incident severity and comms requirements. [1][2]

6. **Verify and document.** For Hosted, the pipeline procedure specifies 5xx below 0.5% for 10 minutes, TTFT p95 within 10% of the 7-day baseline, and GPU OOMs back to baseline or zero. Keep the incident open until metrics are stable for 30 minutes for Hosted or 60 minutes for Dedicated. Record affected regions/clusters, old and new tags, job URLs, times, and verification results. [1][2]
